proofs.proof_tex:
We give an explicit two-witness certificate.  Choose
\[
d=1,\qquad s=7,\qquad \delta=\frac14,\qquad
c_{\theta}=C_{\theta}=c_p=C_p=c_g=C_g=1,
\qquad v_{\kappa}=V_{\kappa}=\frac1{100},\qquad B=2.
\]
Then \(d\) is a positive integer, \(s=7>3(d+1)=6\), and
\(\delta\in(0,1/2)\).  The choices give
\[
c_{\theta}\le C_{\theta},\qquad
c_p\le 1\le C_p,\qquad
c_g\le 1\le C_g,\qquad
v_{\kappa}\le V_{\kappa},
\]
as required by the four ordering compatibility assumptions.  Moreover,
\[
\frac{c_{\theta}}2+\sqrt{v_{\kappa}}
=\frac12+\frac1{10}=\frac35<2=B,
\]
which verifies \(\texttt{ass:bounded-witness-compatibility}\).  Every polynomial used below, and each polynomial entering the definition of \(L_0\), has a finite \(C^s\) norm on its compact domain.  Choose the fixed radius \(L\) at least as large as \(L_0\) and the \(C^s\) norms of the four observed-law primitives displayed below.  This verifies \(\texttt{ass:radius-compatibility}\) and will verify all four smoothness conditions.

On a probability space let \(W\), \(A\), and \(R\) be mutually independent, let \(W\) and \(A\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), and let
\[
\Pr(R=1)=\Pr(R=-1)=\frac12.
\]
Define
\[
Y=A+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10},
\]
and let \(P\) be the law of \((W,A,Y)\).  Since
\[
0\le Y\le \frac65<B,
\]
the law \(P\) satisfies \(\texttt{ass:outcome-bound}\).  Independence and the uniform laws give the everywhere-defined density versions
\[
p(w)=1,\qquad g(a\mid w)=1,\qquad f(a)=\int_0^1g(a\mid w)p(w)\,dw=1.
\]
Consequently
\[
\int_0^1p(w)\,dw=1,
\qquad
\int_0^1g(a\mid w)\,da=1
\quad\text{for every }w\in[0,1],
\]
so \(\texttt{ass:p-normalization}\) and \(\texttt{ass:g-normalization}\) hold.  The equalities \(p=g=1\), together with the chosen constants, also give
\[
c_p\le p(w)\le C_p,
\qquad
c_g\le g(a\mid w)\le C_g,
\]
on their full domains, proving \(\texttt{ass:p-bounds}\) and \(\texttt{ass:overlap}\).

Direct conditioning, using \(\mathbb E[R]=0\) and \(R^2=1\), gives the everywhere-defined versions
\[
m(a,w)=a+\frac1{10},
\qquad
r(a,w)=\left(a+\frac1{10}\right)^2+\frac1{100}.
\]
The functions \(p\), \(g\), \(m\), and \(r\) are polynomials and belong to their respective radius-\(L\) Hölder balls by the choice of \(L\).  Thus \(\texttt{ass:p-smooth}\), \(\texttt{ass:g-smooth}\), \(\texttt{ass:m-smooth}\), and \(\texttt{ass:r-smooth}\) hold.  By the definition of the observed G-computation curve and the normalization of \(p\),
\[
\theta(a)=\int_0^1m(a,w)p(w)\,dw
=a+\frac1{10}
\quad\text{for every }a\in[0,1].
\]
It follows that \(\theta\) is nondecreasing, proving \(\texttt{ass:monotone}\), and that
\[
\theta'(a)=1,
\qquad
c_{\theta}\le\theta'(a)\le C_{\theta}
\quad\text{for every }a\in J=[1/4,3/4],
\]
proving \(\texttt{ass:strict-slope}\).

The definitions of \(\sigma^2\) and \(e\) yield
\[
\sigma^2(a,w)=r(a,w)-m(a,w)^2=\frac1{100},
\qquad
e(a,w)=\frac{g(a\mid w)}{f(a)}=1.
\]
In particular, the division defining \(e\) is legitimate because \(f(a)=1>0\).  From the definitions of \(\xi\) and \(\varepsilon\),
\[
\varepsilon(O)=\frac{Y-m(A,W)}{e(A,W)}=\frac1{10}R.
\]
Therefore the constant version of the conditional second moment is
\[
\kappa(a)=\mathbb E_P\!\left[\varepsilon(O)^2\mid A=a\right]
=\frac1{100}
=v_{\kappa}=V_{\kappa}
\quad\text{for every }a\in J,
\]
which proves \(\texttt{ass:variance}\).

It remains to construct two full-data extensions of this same observed law.  For every \(a\in[0,1]\), define
\[
Y_1(a)=a+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10},
\qquad
Y_2(a)=a+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}\mathbf 1\{a=A\}.
\]
The map \((a,A,R)\mapsto Y_1(a)\) is Borel measurable.  The same is true for \(Y_2\), because the diagonal \(\{(a,A):a=A\}\) is closed and hence Borel.  Thus each sample path is Borel measurable, and all coordinate evaluations are measurable, so each \(Y_j(\cdot)\) is a random element of the evaluation-sigma-field space \(\mathcal Y_B\).  Furthermore,
\[
-\frac1{10}\le Y_j(a)\le\frac65<B
\quad\text{for every }a\in[0,1]
\quad\text{and }j\in\{1,2\},
\]
so both potential-outcome processes take values in the required range \([-B,B]\).

For \(j\in\{1,2\}\), let \(P_j^{\mathrm F}\) be the law of
\[
\bigl(W,A,Y,\{Y_j(a):a\in[0,1]\}\bigr).
\]
By construction, the \((W,A,Y)\)-marginal of each \(P_j^{\mathrm F}\) is \(P\), proving \(\texttt{ass:observed-marginal}\).  At the realized dose,
\[
Y_1(A)=A+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}=Y
\]
and
\[
Y_2(A)=A+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}\mathbf 1\{A=A\}=Y.
\]
Hence both extensions satisfy \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\).

Fix any deterministic \(a\in[0,1]\).  Since \(A\) has a Lebesgue density,
\[
\Pr(A=a)=0.
\]
It follows that
\[
Y_1(a)=a+\frac1{10}R+\frac1{10}
\quad\text{almost surely},
\qquad
Y_2(a)=a+\frac1{10}R
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
Each right-hand side is a measurable function of \(R\), whereas \(R\) is independent of \((A,W)\).  Thus, for every pair of bounded Borel functions \(h\) and \(q\),
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[h\{Y_j(a)\}q(A)\mid W\right]
=\mathbb E\!\left[h\{Y_j(a)\}\mid W\right]
 \mathbb E\!\left[q(A)\mid W\right]
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
This conditional factorization proves \(Y_j(a)\perp A\mid W\) for every deterministic \(a\), so both extensions satisfy \(\texttt{ass:exchangeability}\).

Because \(\mathbb E[R]=0\), define
\[
\mu^{\mathrm F}_1(a,w)=a+\frac1{10},
\qquad
\mu^{\mathrm F}_2(a,w)=a.
\]
These functions are jointly Borel measurable and, for every \(w\), are continuous in \(a\).  For each fixed \(a\), the preceding almost-sure formulas and independence of \(R\) and \(W\) show that
\[
\mu^{\mathrm F}_j(a,W)
=\mathbb E_{P_j^{\mathrm F}}[Y_j(a)\mid W]
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
They are therefore versions satisfying every clause of \(\texttt{ass:potential-mean-continuity}\).

All remaining conditions in \(\texttt{def:model-class}\) are observed-law conditions already verified above.  Hence \(P\in\mathcal M\), and both \(P_1^{\mathrm F}\) and \(P_2^{\mathrm F}\) are admissible full-data witnesses for this same member \(P\).  Finally, for every \(a\in J\),
\[
\mathbb E_{P_1^{\mathrm F}}[Y_1(a)]
=a+\frac1{10}=\theta(a),
\]
whereas
\[
\mathbb E_{P_2^{\mathrm F}}[Y_2(a)]
=a\ne a+\frac1{10}=\theta(a).
\]
The modification defining \(Y_2\) lies on the random diagonal \(a=A\).  It is null in every deterministic-dose section, so it does not alter sectionwise exchangeability or the continuous conditional-mean versions, while consistency evaluates the process precisely on that diagonal.  This proves the stated failure of exact-dose causal identification under the frozen model.

Put \(D_0=d+1\) and \(h_n=n^{-1/(2s)}\), as in the statement.  For \(j=0\), the bias term in the assumed implementation bound is
\[
 h_n^s=\left(n^{-1/(2s)}\right)^s=n^{-1/2},
\]
whereas its stochastic term is
\[
 \left(\frac{\log n}{n h_n^{D_0}}\right)^{1/2}
 =n^{-1/2+D_0/(4s)}\sqrt{\log n}
 =n^{-\beta}\sqrt{\log n},
 \qquad
 \beta=\frac12-\frac{d+1}{4s}.
\]
Because \(D_0=d+1>0\), one has \(\beta<1/2\), so the stochastic term is no smaller in order than \(n^{-1/2}\).  The conditional rate premise in the lemma therefore gives, for each \(h\in\{g,m,r\}\),
\[
 \max_{1\le k\le K}\lVert\widehat h_k-h\rVert_\infty
 =O_P\!\left(n^{-\beta}\sqrt{\log n}\right).
\]
For \(p\), the stipulated analogue has dimension \(d<D_0\); its stochastic exponent is \(1/2-d/(4s)>\beta\), and its bias is again \(n^{-1/2}\).  Thus its rate is bounded by the same displayed order.  Finally, the model restriction \(s>3(d+1)\) yields
\[
 \beta=\frac12-\frac{d+1}{4s}
 >\frac12-\frac1{12}=\frac5{12}.
\]

For \(j=1\), direct substitution gives
\[
 h_n^{s-1}=n^{-1/2+1/(2s)}
\]
and
\[
 \left(\frac{\log n}{n h_n^{D_0+2}}\right)^{1/2}
 =n^{-1/2+(d+3)/(4s)}\sqrt{\log n}
 =n^{-\beta_1}\sqrt{\log n},
 \qquad
 \beta_1=\frac12-\frac{d+3}{4s}.
\]
The latter term is the slower one, since
\[
 \left(\frac12-\frac1{2s}\right)-\beta_1
 =\frac{d+1}{4s}>0.
\]
Moreover, again using \(s>3(d+1)\),
\[
 \beta_1
 >\frac12-\frac{d+3}{12(d+1)}
 =\frac{5d+3}{12(d+1)}>0.
\]
Consequently the assumed first-derivative implementation bound gives
\[
 \max_{1\le k\le K}
 \lVert\partial_a\widehat m_k-\partial_a m\rVert_\infty
 =O_P\!\left(n^{-\beta_1}\sqrt{\log n}\right).
\]

It remains to pass this rate to the derivative of the plug-in dose-response curve.  Assumption \(\texttt{ass:m-smooth}\) makes \(\partial_a m\) continuous and uniformly bounded by a constant determined by the fixed radius \(L\).  Hence differentiation under the integral is valid on the compact domain, and
\[
 \theta'(a)=\int_{[0,1]^d}\partial_a m(a,w)p(w)\,dw.
\]
For each fold, nonnegativity and unit-mass normalization of \(\widehat p_k\), together with \(\texttt{ass:p-normalization}\), give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left|\int\partial_a\widehat m_k(a,w)\widehat p_k(w)\,dw-
             \theta'(a)\right|
 &\le
 \int\left|\partial_a\widehat m_k(a,w)-\partial_a m(a,w)\right|
       \widehat p_k(w)\,dw\\
 &\quad+
 \int\left|\partial_a m(a,w)\right|
       \left|\widehat p_k(w)-p(w)\right|\,dw\\
 &\le
 \lVert\partial_a\widehat m_k-\partial_a m\rVert_\infty
 +\lVert\partial_a m\rVert_\infty
  \lVert\widehat p_k-p\rVert_1.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The covariate cube has Lebesgue volume one, so
\(\lVert\widehat p_k-p\rVert_1\le
\lVert\widehat p_k-p\rVert_\infty\).  Since
\(\beta-\beta_1=1/(2s)>0\), the zeroth-order density error is of no larger order than the first-derivative error.  Taking the supremum over \(a\in J\), then the maximum over the fixed number \(K\) of folds, proves
\[
 \lVert\widehat\theta'-\theta'\rVert_{\infty,J}
 =O_P\!\left(n^{-\beta_1}\sqrt{\log n}\right);
\]
averaging the foldwise plug-ins cannot increase this bound.  Every stochastic order used here is an explicit premise of the conditional implementation statement, so the calculation makes no probability assertion about an otherwise unspecified learner.

Write
\[
 a_n=n^{-\beta}\sqrt{\log n}.
\]
By the definition of \(\mathfrak B_n\) and the conditional zeroth-order conclusions of \(\texttt{lem:learner-rates}\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathfrak B_n
 &\le
 \max_{1\le k\le K}\lVert\widehat m_k-m\rVert_\infty
 \left(
   \max_{1\le k\le K}\lVert\widehat g_k-g\rVert_\infty
   +\max_{1\le k\le K}\lVert\widehat p_k-p\rVert_\infty
 \right)\\
 &=O_P(a_n^2)
 =O_P\!\left(n^{-2\beta}\log n\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
It follows that
\[
 n^{5/6}(\log n)^{3/2}\mathfrak B_n
 =O_P\!\left(n^{5/6-2\beta}(\log n)^{5/2}\right).
\]
The exponent of \(n\) equals
\[
 \frac56-2\beta
 =-\frac16+\frac{d+1}{2s}<0,
\]
where the strict inequality is exactly \(s>3(d+1)\).  A negative power of \(n\) dominates the fixed logarithmic power, which proves
\[
 n^{5/6}(\log n)^{3/2}\mathfrak B_n=o_P(1).
\]

We next justify the two plug-in bounds.  Assumptions \(\texttt{ass:p-normalization}\) and \(\texttt{ass:overlap}\) imply, for every \(a\in[0,1]\),
\[
 c_g
 =c_g\int p(w)\,dw
 \le f(a)=\int g(a\mid w)p(w)\,dw
 \le C_g\int p(w)\,dw=C_g.
\]
For a nonnegative unit-mass density estimate, addition and subtraction of
\(\int g(a\mid w)\widehat p(w)\,dw\) give
\[
 \lVert\widehat f-f\rVert_\infty
 \le \lVert\widehat g-g\rVert_\infty
     +C_g\lVert\widehat p-p\rVert_1
 =O_P(a_n).
\]
Assumption \(\texttt{ass:outcome-bound}\) gives \(|m|\le B\) and
\(0\le r\le B^2\).  On an event whose probability tends to one, the conditional learner rates therefore put \(\widehat m\), \(\widehat r\), \(\widehat g\), and \(\widehat p\) in a fixed bounded neighborhood of their true values, while the denominator-safe premise and \(g\ge c_g\) keep every treatment-density denominator bounded away from zero.  On that event,
\[
 \lVert(\widehat r-\widehat m^2)-(r-m^2)\rVert_\infty
 \le \lVert\widehat r-r\rVert_\infty
   +\lVert\widehat m-m\rVert_\infty
    \lVert\widehat m+m\rVert_\infty
 =O_P(a_n).
\]
Addition, multiplication, and reciprocal maps are Lipschitz on this fixed compact range, and integration over the unit cube is a contraction from the supremum norm to the absolute value.  Applying these facts successively to
\[
 \kappa(a)
 =f(a)\int
 \frac{\{r(a,w)-m(a,w)^2\}p(w)}{g(a\mid w)}\,dw
\]
and its denominator-safe plug-in version yields
\[
 \lVert\widehat\kappa-\kappa\rVert_{\infty,J}=O_P(a_n).
\]
The fixed lower bound \(\kappa(a)\ge v_\kappa\) in \(\texttt{ass:variance}\) now gives
\[
 \mathfrak K_n
 =\sup_{a\in J}\left|\frac{\widehat\kappa(a)}{\kappa(a)}-1\right|
 \le v_\kappa^{-1}
      \lVert\widehat\kappa-\kappa\rVert_{\infty,J}
 =O_P\!\left(n^{-\beta}\sqrt{\log n}\right).
\]

For the clock, define
\[
 \psi(x,y,z)=\left(\frac{xy^2}{4z}\right)^{1/3}.
\]
By \(\texttt{ass:strict-slope}\), \(\texttt{ass:variance}\), and the preceding bounds on \(f\), the true triple \((f(a),\theta'(a),\kappa(a))\) ranges over the compact rectangle
\[
 [c_g,C_g]\times[c_\theta,C_\theta]\times[v_\kappa,V_\kappa].
\]
The function \(\psi\) is continuously differentiable, and hence Lipschitz, on a fixed neighborhood of this rectangle.  The conditional learner rates imply that the plug-in triple lies in that neighborhood with probability tending to one; on this event the stabilizations are inactive for all sufficiently large \(n\).  Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left|\widehat{\mathcal V}_n-\mathcal V(P)\right|
 &\le C\int_J
 \left(
  |\widehat f(a)-f(a)|
  +|\widehat\theta'(a)-\theta'(a)|
  +|\widehat\kappa(a)-\kappa(a)|
 \right)\,da\\
 &=O_P\!\left(n^{-\beta_1}\sqrt{\log n}
              +n^{-\beta}\sqrt{\log n}\right),
 \end{aligned}
\]
where \(C<\infty\) depends only on the fixed model constants.  The same three assumptions also give the deterministic lower bound
\[
 \mathcal V(P)
 \ge |J|\left(\frac{c_g c_\theta^2}{4V_\kappa}\right)^{1/3}>0;
\]
here \(|J|=1-2\delta>0\) because \(\delta\in(0,1/2)\).  Division by this lower bound proves
\[
 \left|\frac{\widehat{\mathcal V}_n}{\mathcal V(P)}-1\right|
 =O_P\!\left(n^{-\beta_1}\sqrt{\log n}
              +n^{-\beta}\sqrt{\log n}\right).
\]

We now prove the fixed-kernel validation calculation and keep its lack of uniformity explicit.  Let a validation fold have size \(N\asymp n\), let \(I\) have length \(h\), and let \(\phi\) be the fixed bounded continuously differentiable kernel in the statement.  Set
\[
 \mu(a)=\int\phi(a,w)p(w)\,dw,
 \qquad
 H(O_i,O_j)=\mathbf 1\{A_i\in I\}
       \{\phi(A_i,W_j)-\mu(A_i)\}.
\]
For \(i\ne j\), independence from \(\texttt{ass:iid}\) and the definition of \(\mu\) give
\[
 \mathbb E_P\{H(O_i,O_j)\mid O_i\}=0.
\]
The other projection is
\[
 q_I(w)=\mathbb E_P\!\left[
   \mathbf 1\{A\in I\}\{\phi(A,w)-\mu(A)\}
 \right].
\]
Since \(f\le C_g\),
\[
 \lVert q_I\rVert_\infty
 \le 2\lVert\phi\rVert_\infty P(A\in I)
 \le 2\lVert\phi\rVert_\infty C_g h,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P q_I(W)=0.
\]
Thus the projection average has variance at most a constant times \(h^2/N\), and consequently is \(O_P(h/\sqrt N)\) by the elementary bound
\(P(|X|>t)\le \mathbb E(X^2)/t^2\) for centered \(X\).

Subtracting \(q_I(W_j)\) from \(H(O_i,O_j)\) produces a kernel degenerate in each argument.  Its second moment is \(O(h)\), because the squared \(H\)-term is bounded and vanishes unless \(A_i\in I\), while \(q_I(W_j)^2=O(h^2)\).  Expanding the square of its ordered-pair average, degeneracy makes every covariance vanish unless the two ordered pairs coincide or are reversals.  There are only \(O(N^2)\) such terms, so
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left{
  \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i\ne j}
  \bigl[H(O_i,O_j)-q_I(W_j)\bigr]
 \right}
 =O\!\left(\frac{h}{N^2}\right).
\]
The degenerate part is therefore \(O_P(\sqrt h/N)\).  If the corresponding all-pairs statistic is used, its \(N\) diagonal summands are uniformly bounded and their contribution after division by \(N^2\) is \(O(N^{-1})\).  Combining the projection, degenerate, and diagonal bounds, and using \(N\asymp n\), proves the asserted order
\[
 O_P\!\left(\frac h{\sqrt n}+\frac{\sqrt h}{n}+\frac1n\right).
\]
For example, at the frozen width \(h=H_n=n^{-1/3}(\log n)^2\), multiplication by \(n^{2/3}\sqrt{\log n}\) sends the three terms respectively to
\[
 n^{-1/6}(\log n)^{5/2},\qquad
 n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{3/2},\qquad
 n^{-1/3}(\log n)^{1/2},
\]
all of which tend to zero.  This calculation is for a fixed \(I\) and fixed \(\phi\); it does not take a supremum over fitted kernels or intervals.

Finally, consider a fixed compact optimization interval and write
\[
 L_X(v)=\int v(t)^2\,dt-2\int v\,dX.
\]
Let \(H=X-\widetilde X\), assume \(\lVert H\rVert_\infty\le\eta\), and let \(v\) belong to either monotone optimization class.  Its assumed envelope gives \(\lVert v\rVert_\infty\le M_0\), and monotonicity gives
\(\operatorname{TV}(v)\le2M_0\).  Stieltjes integration by parts, including both endpoint terms, therefore yields
\[
 \left|\int v\,dH\right|
 \le \eta\{\operatorname{TV}(v)+2M_0\}
 \le4M_0\eta.
\]
Consequently
\[
 |L_X(v)-L_{\widetilde X}(v)|
 =2\left|\int v\,dH\right|
 \le8M_0\eta.
\]
For either optimization class \(\mathcal C\), the elementary inequality
\[
 \left|\inf_{v\in\mathcal C}L_X(v)
       -\inf_{v\in\mathcal C}L_{\widetilde X}(v)\right|
 \le\sup_{v\in\mathcal C}|L_X(v)-L_{\widetilde X}(v)|
\]
then bounds the change in its optimized value by \(8M_0\eta\).  Taking the difference between the constrained and unconstrained optimized values and applying the triangle inequality proves the stated \(16M_0\eta\) bound.

The last two arguments use, respectively, a fixed kernel and a common compact optimization interval with a common slope envelope.  Neither argument supplies a fitted-kernel maximal inequality, common contact localization, or such an envelope from the four scalar clauses in \(\mathsf G_n\).  Hence the proved calculations do not yield \(S_n-S_n^\circ=o_P(1)\); that transfer would require the additional missing controls identified in the statement.

Fix \(x\in\mathbb R\) and define
\[
 \mathbb W_x(t)=\mathbb W(x+t)-\mathbb W(x),\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
\]
By \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\),
\[
 X(x+t)-X(x)-2xt=\mathbb W_x(t)+t^2. \tag{1}
\]
We first verify the pathwise equivariance used in (1). If \(G\) is the greatest convex minorant of a function \(F\), then
\[
 \widetilde G(t)=G(x+t)-G(x)-2xt
\]
is the greatest convex minorant of \(\widetilde F(t)=F(x+t)-F(x)-2xt\). Indeed, \(\widetilde G\) is convex and lies below \(\widetilde F\); applying the inverse translation and affine addition to any convex minorant of \(\widetilde F\) produces a convex minorant of \(F\), hence one bounded above by \(G\). The same argument on each half-line proves equivariance of the one-sided constrained minorants. Under this transformation the slope constraint \(2x\) becomes the origin constraint \(0\), and every slope is reduced by \(2x\). Changing variables \(s=x+t\) in the energy integral therefore gives
\[
 D(x)=\Phi(\mathbb W_x). \tag{2}
\]

The independent stationary Gaussian increment property in \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\) gives \(\mathbb W_x\stackrel{d}{=}\mathbb W\). Since \(D(0)=\Phi(\mathbb W)\), (2) implies
\[
 D(x)\stackrel{d}{=}D(0). \tag{3}
\]
By \(\texttt{lem:banerjee-wellner-fixed-location-lr}\), \(D(0)\) is finite and nonnegative almost surely. Thus (3) gives the same conclusion at every fixed \(x\). Intersecting the resulting probability-one events for a finite deterministic collection \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) proves their simultaneous finiteness and nonnegativity.

For joint stationarity, fix \(x_1,\ldots,x_m,r\in\mathbb R\). The centered Gaussian vector process
\[
 \bigl(\mathbb W_{x_1+r}(t),\ldots,\mathbb W_{x_m+r}(t):t\in\mathbb R\bigr)
\]
has the same covariance function as
\[
 \bigl(\mathbb W_{x_1}(t),\ldots,\mathbb W_{x_m}(t):t\in\mathbb R\bigr).
\]
Every covariance on either side is the covariance of two Brownian increments, and translating all four increment endpoints by \(r\) leaves their signed overlap unchanged. The two vector processes have mean zero, so their finite-dimensional laws coincide. Applying the measurable fixed-location GCM-energy map in (2) coordinatewise yields
\[
 (D(x_1+r),\ldots,D(x_m+r))\stackrel{d}{=}
 (D(x_1),\ldots,D(x_m)).
\]
Only finitely many fixed-location maps were used, so this proves none of the expressly excluded continuum regularity or block-independence properties.

For a deterministic perturbation \(h\), write \(F_h(t)=t^2+h(t)\). For \(h_b(t)=b^2h(t/b)\),
\[
 F_{h_b}(t)=b^2F_h(t/b). \tag{1}
\]
If \(G_h\) is the unrestricted greatest convex minorant of \(F_h\), then \(t\mapsto b^2G_h(t/b)\) is convex and lies below the right-hand side of (1). Conversely, applying the inverse dilation to any convex minorant of \(F_{h_b}\) produces a convex minorant of \(F_h\). Hence
\[
 G_{h_b}(t)=b^2G_h(t/b). \tag{2}
\]
The same order argument on the left and right half-lines proves (2) for the origin-constrained minorants. All corresponding slopes are multiplied by \(b\). Substitution of \(t=bs\) into the difference of squared-slope energies in \(\texttt{def:excursion-regime}\) gives
\[
 \Phi(h_b)=b^3\Phi(h). \tag{3}
\]
This proves the first identity whenever the relevant energies are defined.

If \(h\) is absolutely continuous, \(h_b'(t)=b h'(t/b)\) almost everywhere. Since \(h'\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), the same substitution gives
\[
 \frac12\lVert h_b'\rVert_2^2
 =\frac12\int_{\mathbb R}b^2\{h'(t/b)\}^2dt
 =b^3\frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2. \tag{4}
\]

Fix \(u>0\), and put \(b=u^{1/3}\) and \(\epsilon=u^{-1/2}=b^{-3/2}\). The mean and covariance of two-sided Brownian motion give
\[
 b^{1/2}\mathbb W(\,\cdot\,/b)\stackrel{d}{=}\mathbb W
\]
as two-sided continuous processes, while
\[
 (\epsilon\mathbb W)_b(t)=b^2\epsilon\mathbb W(t/b)
 =b^{1/2}\mathbb W(t/b).
\]
Using the fixed-location measurability and well-posedness from \(\texttt{lem:canonical-wellposedness}\), the identity \(D(0)=\Phi(\mathbb W)\) from \(\texttt{def:canonical-field}\), and (3), we obtain
\[
 D(0)\stackrel{d}{=}\Phi((\epsilon\mathbb W)_b)
 =b^3\Phi(\epsilon\mathbb W)
 =u\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W).
\]
Therefore
\[
 \Pr\{D(0)>u\}=\Pr\{\Phi(u^{-1/2}\mathbb W)>1\}. \tag{5}
\]

We next prove the deterministic action bound. Let \(h(0)=0\), \(h'\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), and set
\[
 \ell(t)=2t,\qquad y(t)=\ell(t)+h'(t).
\]
Let \(\mathcal C\) be the convex set of nondecreasing slope functions and let \(\mathcal C_0\subset\mathcal C\) impose the origin split constraint \(q(t)\le0\) for \(t<0\) and \(q(t)\ge0\) for \(t>0\). For \(q-\ell\in L^2(\mathbb R)\), define
\[
 Q_h(q)=\int_{\mathbb R}\left[\{q(t)-\ell(t)\}^2
 -2h'(t)\{q(t)-\ell(t)\}\right]dt. \tag{6}
\]
The unrestricted and constrained GCM slopes minimize (6) over \(\mathcal C\) and \(\mathcal C_0\), respectively. To verify this directly, first work on a finite interval. If \(G\) is the GCM of a primitive of \(y\), \(g=G'\), and \(H=F_h-G\), then \(H\ge0\), the measure \(dg\) is carried by \(\{H=0\}\), and integration by parts gives, for each nondecreasing competitor \(v\),
\[
 \int (y-g)(v-g)
 =-\int H\,dv+\int H\,dg\le0. \tag{7}
\]
The endpoint term is zero because the greatest convex minorant meets the primitive at the relevant endpoints. The same calculation on the two half-intervals, with the cap and floor at zero, gives (7) for the constrained slope. Exhaustion by finite intervals and \(L^2\)-approximation give (7) on \(\mathbb R\). Expanding squared distances shows that (7) is exactly the variational condition for minimizing (6). The same expansion together with the contact identity gives
\[
 \Phi(h)=Q_h(g^0)-Q_h(g), \tag{8}
\]
where \(g\) and \(g^0\) are the unrestricted and constrained GCM slopes. Because \(\mathcal C_0\subset\mathcal C\), (8) is nonnegative.

The baseline \(\ell\) belongs to \(\mathcal C_0\), and \(Q_h(\ell)=0\). Thus the constrained minimum is at most zero. For \(q=\ell+z\), completing the square in (6) gives
\[
 Q_h(q)=\lVert z-h'\rVert_2^2-\lVert h'\rVert_2^2
 \ge-\lVert h'\rVert_2^2. \tag{9}
\]
Equations (8)--(9) imply
\[
 0\le\Phi(h)\le\lVert h'\rVert_2^2. \tag{10}
\]
Thus \(\Phi(h)\ge1\) entails \(\frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2\ge\frac12\). Taking the infimum in \(\texttt{def:excursion-regime}\) proves
\[
 I_\star\ge\frac12. \tag{11}
\]

For the upper bound, let \(k=4^{1/3}\), \(a=k/4\), and define the absolutely continuous \(h\) by \(h(0)=0\) and
\[
 h'(t)=(k-2t)\mathbf 1\{-a\le t\le k/2\}. \tag{12}
\]
This derivative has compact support and belongs to \(L^2(\mathbb R)\). The derivative of \(F_h\) is
\[
 y(t)=2t+h'(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 2t,&t<-a,\\
 k,&-a\le t\le k/2,\\
 2t,&t>k/2.
 \end{cases} \tag{13}
\]
Because \(-2a=-k/2<k\) and \(2(k/2)=k\), (13) is nondecreasing. Hence \(F_h\) is convex and its unrestricted GCM slope is \(y\). Define
\[
 z(t)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&-a\le t\le0,\\
 y(t),&t\notin[-a,0].
 \end{cases}
\]
The function \(z\) is nondecreasing and satisfies the origin split constraint. Every other constrained slope \(v\) obeys \(v(t)\le0=z(t)\) on \([-a,0]\), whereas \(y-z=0\) off that interval. Therefore
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}(y-z)(v-z)dt
 =k\int_{-a}^{0}v(t)dt\le0. \tag{14}
\]
Expanding the difference of the squared residual norms shows from (14) that \(z\) is the constrained quadratic minimizer and hence the constrained GCM slope. Consequently,
\[
 \Phi(h)=\int_{-a}^{0}k^2dt=ak^2=\frac{k^3}{4}=1. \tag{15}
\]
Finally, (12), \(a=k/4\), and \(k^3=4\) give
\[
 \frac12\lVert h'\rVert_2^2
 =\frac12\int_{-a}^{k/2}(k-2t)^2dt
 =\frac{(k+2a)^3}{12}
 =\frac{(3k/2)^3}{12}=\frac98. \tag{16}
\]
This admissible unit-energy witness proves \(I_\star\le9/8\); together with (11), this is the stated bracket. The argument supplies no large-deviation limit or probability-tail rate.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\) and \(a\in J\). By \(\texttt{ass:p-normalization}\), \(\int p(w)\,dw=1\), and by \(\texttt{ass:overlap}\), \(c_g\le g(a\mid w)\le C_g\). Since \(p\ge0\), the definition of \(f\) gives
\[
 c_g=c_g\int p(w)\,dw
 \le f(a)=\int g(a\mid w)p(w)\,dw
 \le C_g\int p(w)\,dw=C_g. \tag{1}
\]
The assumptions \(\texttt{ass:strict-slope}\) and \(\texttt{ass:variance}\) give
\[
 0<c_\theta\le\theta'(a)\le C_\theta,
 \qquad
 0<v_\kappa\le\kappa(a)\le V_\kappa. \tag{2}
\]
Thus all factors divided by in \(h_n(a)\) are positive. Combining (1)--(2), with division only by positive quantities, yields
\[
 \left(\frac{4v_\kappa}{nC_gC_\theta^2}\right)^{1/3}
 \le h_n(a)\le
 \left(\frac{4V_\kappa}{nc_gc_\theta^2}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{3}
\]
Multiplication by \(n^{1/3}>0\) proves the first displayed bound in the theorem.

Inverting the positive definition gives
\[
 h_n(a)^{-1}=n^{1/3}
 \left\{\frac{f(a)\theta'(a)^2}{4\kappa(a)}\right\}^{1/3}. \tag{4}
\]
Taking reciprocals in (3) places (4) between
\[
 n^{1/3}\left(\frac{c_gc_\theta^2}{4V_\kappa}\right)^{1/3}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 n^{1/3}\left(\frac{C_gC_\theta^2}{4v_\kappa}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{5}
\]
For \(a_1<a_2\) in \(J\), integration of (5) gives positive finite constants \(c_n,C_n\) such that
\[
 c_n(a_2-a_1)\le
 \Psi_{n,P}(a_2)-\Psi_{n,P}(a_1)
 \le C_n(a_2-a_1). \tag{6}
\]
Hence \(\Psi_{n,P}\) is strictly increasing and bi-Lipschitz. Since \(\Psi_{n,P}(\inf J)=0\), its image is an interval of length \(\Psi_{n,P}(\sup J)\). Integrating (4) and invoking \(\texttt{def:spatial-clock}\) proves
\[
 \Psi_{n,P}(\sup J)
 =n^{1/3}\int_J
 \left\{\frac{f(a)\theta'(a)^2}{4\kappa(a)}\right\}^{1/3}da
 =n^{1/3}\mathcal V(P)=T_n(P). \tag{7}
\]
The constants in (3) and (5) use only fixed model constants, so the assertions are uniform over \(P\in\mathcal M\) and \(a\in J\). No stochastic approximation was used.

Under the three positive constant-coefficient hypotheses, substitution into \(\texttt{def:spatial-clock}\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal V(P)
 &=\int_J\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3}da
 =|J|\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3},\\
 T_n(P)
 &=n^{1/3}\mathcal V(P)
 =n^{1/3}|J|\left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3}.
 \end{aligned} \tag{1}
\]
The inverse scale from \(\texttt{thm:causal-transfer}\) is constant in \(a\):
\[
 h_n(a)^{-1}=n^{1/3}
 \left(\frac{f_0r_0^2}{4\kappa_0}\right)^{1/3}. \tag{2}
\]
Integrating (2) from \(\inf J\) to \(a\) makes \(\Psi_{n,P}\) affine, with total image length equal to (1).

For the fixed-location assertion, take \(m=1\), \(x_1=0\), and \(r=x\) in \(\texttt{lem:canonical-wellposedness}\). It gives
\[
 D(x)\stackrel{d}{=}D(0). \tag{3}
\]
That lemma derives (3) by translating the constraint and subtracting the affine tangent, which is exactly translation and affine GCM equivariance. Equations (1)--(3) contain no growing-domain or calibration conclusion.

Fix a realized sample, fix \(a\in J\), and abbreviate \(k=k(a)\), \(z_i=Z_{(i)}\), and
\[
 F(v)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(z_i-v_i)^2,
 \qquad
 L_k(t)=\min\{F(v):v\in\mathcal C_n,\ v_k=t\}.
\]
For every \(t\in\mathbb R\), the feasible set
\[
 H_k(t)=\{v\in\mathcal C_n:v_k=t\}
\]
is nonempty because it contains the constant vector \(t\mathbf 1\).  It is closed because \(\mathcal C_n\) is closed by \(\texttt{def:lr-profile}\) and the coordinate constraint is closed.  Moreover, \(F(v)=\lVert v-z\rVert_2^2\) is continuous and coercive.  Hence its minimum over \(H_k(t)\) is attained and finite.  The unrestricted minimum
\[
 c_0=\min_{v\in\mathcal C_n}F(v)=F(\widehat u)
\]
is likewise attained, and the definitions in \(\texttt{def:lr-profile}\) give
\[
 Q_n(a,t)=L_k(t)-c_0.
\]
In particular, \(Q_n(a,t)\ge 0\), since the constrained feasible set is a subset of \(\mathcal C_n\).

To prove convexity, take \(t_1,t_2\in\mathbb R\), choose minimizers \(v^{(j)}\in H_k(t_j)\), and let \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).  Convexity of \(\mathcal C_n\) yields
\[
 \lambda v^{(1)}+(1-\lambda)v^{(2)}\in
 H_k\bigl(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda)t_2\bigr).
\]
Convexity of the squared norm therefore implies
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 L_k\bigl(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda)t_2\bigr)
 &\le F\bigl(\lambda v^{(1)}+(1-\lambda)v^{(2)}\bigr)\\
 &\le \lambda F(v^{(1)})+(1-\lambda)F(v^{(2)})\\
 &=\lambda L_k(t_1)+(1-\lambda)L_k(t_2).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(L_k\), and hence \(t\mapsto Q_n(a,t)\), is convex.  Since \(L_k\) is finite on all of \(\mathbb R\), it is continuous on \(\mathbb R\).  Also, because the \(k\)-th summand of \(F\) equals \((z_k-t)^2\) on \(H_k(t)\),
\[
 Q_n(a,t)=L_k(t)-c_0\ge (z_k-t)^2-c_0\longrightarrow +\infty
 \quad\text{as }|t|\longrightarrow\infty.
\]

Now realize the measurable threshold \(\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\).  If it is finite, positivity of \(\widehat\kappa(a)\) and nonnegativity of the threshold make
\[
 c(a)=\widehat\kappa(a)\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\in[0,\infty).
\]
The sublevel set \(\{t:Q_n(a,t)\le c(a)\}\) is convex, hence an interval, and is closed by continuity.  It is nonempty because \(t=\widehat u_k\) gives \(L_k(t)=c_0\) and therefore \(Q_n(a,t)=0\); it is bounded by the preceding coercive lower bound.  Thus it is in fact a nonempty compact interval.  If \(\widehat q_{n,\alpha}=+\infty\), finiteness of \(Q_n(a,t)\) for every \(t\) instead gives the whole real line.  This proves the asserted interval structure in \(\texttt{def:profile-band}\).

Let
\[
 E=\{\theta(a)\in\mathcal C_n(a)\text{ for every }a\in J\}.
\]
By \(\texttt{def:profile-band}\), by \(\widehat\kappa(a)>0\), and then by \(\texttt{def:lr-profile}\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E
 &=\left\{\frac{Q_n(a,\theta(a))}{\widehat\kappa(a)}
       \le \widehat q_{n,\alpha}\text{ for every }a\in J\right\}\\
 &=\left\{\sup_{a\in J}
       \frac{Q_n(a,\theta(a))}{\widehat\kappa(a)}
       \le \widehat q_{n,\alpha}\right\}\\
 &=\{S_n(\theta)\le\widehat q_{n,\alpha}\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The middle equivalence is the defining order property of a supremum and remains valid when the threshold equals \(+\infty\).

Finally, on \(E\), the curve \(\theta\) selects a point of \(\mathcal C_n(a)\) for every \(a\in J\), and it is nondecreasing by \(\texttt{ass:monotone}\).  It is therefore one of the curves mapped by \(\texttt{def:crossing-set}\).  The image of this particular selector is
\[
 \inf\{a\in J:\theta(a)\ge\zeta\}=\tau_\zeta,
\]
with exactly the same empty-set and left-endpoint conventions appearing in the definition of \(\tau_\zeta\).  Consequently the crossing-set image contains \(\tau_\zeta\) on \(E\).  All conclusions are deterministic for the realized sample.  In particular, the argument identifies the simultaneous profile event exactly and proves containment on that event, but it assigns no probability, nominal or otherwise, to that event.
